p.t: In short
A **theme** sets how your store looks and works. Products and store content stay the same when you change it.

Upload the theme as a **.zip file**, not a folder. Click **Publish** only when the store is ready.
Only one theme can be live at a time. Uploaded themes stay hidden until you publish them.

Most visitors use phones, so pick a theme that works well on mobile.
A free theme is enough to start. Paid themes are not needed on day one.

Build every change in a **draft** first. The live store stays untouched.
Publishing replaces the live theme at once. Only **publish** when setup is finished.

Make a **backup** before you change any code.
Switching themes keeps your products, but you must **redo** colors, logo and layout.
Do not switch just because a new theme exists. A working store can stay as it is.
**Buy** themes only from the official source or a verified seller. Pirated themes can hide harmful code that breaks your store.
An uploaded theme is seen only by your store team until you publish it (make it live for shoppers).
You can publish a theme while the store is still locked with a password, so you can prepare it first.
When moving to a new store, export and import the theme and lists, then **rebuild** what did not transfer.
Theme basics and where themes sit in Shopify
A **theme** is the design package for your store.
It controls how the store looks, how pages are built, and how customers use the site. Shopify provides the backend (the hidden engine that runs orders, payments and products).
The theme provides the presentation (what visitors see) and the user experience (how it feels to click around).
The theme controls the **storefront** (the shop side that visitors see) and how it behaves. **Products and store content stay the same** when the theme changes.
Themes are installed as ZIP files through the **Shopify admin** (the back office where you run the store).

**Free and paid themes** both change how the storefront looks and works. Products and store content stay the same. A theme is a separate layer from the store's **catalog** (the list of products) and settings.
A theme sets the overall design, the page structure, and how far the store can be customized. Any installed theme can be changed to fit the store.
A theme is a structure and **does not include product images or content**.
A **developer** (a person who writes website code) builds the base theme and supplies all site code.
The store owner adds branding (colors, images, a few settings) through the **theme editor** (the visual tool for changing the look). The owner does not need to code from scratch.
A theme provides the basic site layout and structure. After installing it, add your own **branding** (your name, logo and style), colors, and **fonts** (text styles).
Themes are managed under **Online Store > Themes**. In one source the path is written as Sales channels > Online store > Themes.
The page shows the **active theme** (the one visitors see now) and an **Add theme** button. The **Theme library** (the list of all uploaded themes) sits lower down on the page.
The Themes page has a **Visit theme store** link near the bottom. The theme store lists free and paid themes. **Paid themes are generally better built** than free ones.
The Themes page also links to **Free themes** and the **Shopify Theme Store** (Shopify's official shop for themes).
The **Customize** button opens the theme editor. Most store layout and branding work happens there.
An **unpublished** theme (not yet live for visitors) shows **Customize** and **Actions** buttons. Use Customize only when editing.
A store can hold several uploaded themes, but **only one** can be published and shown to visitors.
The default theme on a new store
New accounts receive the free theme **Dawn**.

It is the active theme from the start and stays active until another theme is published.
Dawn is Shopify's free default theme and a common base for a first store.
The course store in one source used Dawn. The source advised keeping the store simple at first. The **offer** (what you sell and at what price) and product images matter more than design complexity.
The course material of that period says a new store starts with the free theme **Debut**. Debut shows only **placeholder** content (dummy text and images) and no branding.
It must be customized before launch.
Where sources disagree on the default, use **Dawn** for current accounts. Use Debut only for stores described in the older 2021-22 material.

The free default theme without customization looks very basic. Changing only the **header** (the top bar of the page) while leaving default colors in other sections creates an inconsistent look that signals a beginner.
Start with a **lightweight** theme (one that loads fast because it uses little code) for site speed. The 2022 advice recommended the Charlotte theme.
Speed is one of the first things to check. Check a theme on stores that already run it. Run **speed tests** (tools that measure how fast a page loads) on those stores before buying.
Check when the theme was last **updated** and how long its developer has supported it.
Themes untouched for **four or five years** can produce errors with the current Shopify framework (the base system the theme runs on).
Use a **mobile-responsive** theme (one that adjusts its layout to fit phones). **Most purchases now happen on phones.** A web-only theme loses sales to competitors and needs a full rebuild.

**Mobile traffic** (visitors arriving on phones) can be **80 to 90 percent** of visits. The theme should work well on phones out of the box. Mobile-only design changes that differ from desktop need a developer.
Make them only when a specific error or problem appears.
Check every key page at **laptop-width** screens too, as well as desktop and mobile. If the theme stops at a fixed maximum width, the side margins stay cramped.
The **white space** (empty space that keeps a page easy to read) disappears. Choose a theme that scales to wide screens.
Prefer a theme with **minimal, clean code** (little, tidy code). Theme and **app** (an add-on program) code quality varies. Some popular-looking themes are coded inefficiently and slow the page.

Choose a theme with **built-in features**, so fewer third-party apps (add-ons made by other companies) are needed. Fewer apps generally means faster pages and fewer **plugins** (small add-ons) to maintain.
Choosing a theme: criteria (continued)

A **premium** (paid) theme is worth choosing over a free one when it already includes **conversion** elements (parts that help visitors become buyers). The store then needs fewer paid apps for the same features.
Before buying a paid theme, check that it supports the features you need. Examples are **bundles with variants** (one package with size or color options) and **free gift offers**.
Themes that lack these features may force a costly **workaround** (a messy fix).
Give the person building the store **clear written requirements**. Make sure the theme is installed correctly and reviewed before launch. A poorly installed theme can make a store look messy.
Choose the base theme with your planned amount of custom work in mind. A simpler base with fewer built-in features can be easier to customize heavily than a feature-rich theme.
A **dropshipping-focused** theme is built for dropshipping (selling products that a supplier ships to the buyer, so you hold no stock). It can be more efficient than comparing many general themes.
The theme affects both conversion and setup effort. Treat claims about higher conversions as **unverified** (not proven) until you test them on your own store.
**Manhattan** is built specifically for **high-ticket dropshipping** (selling expensive products through suppliers).
It is optimized (tuned) for higher conversions and **supplier-ready presentation** (a look that makes supplier products look good). It includes features that usually need paid apps.
This lowers setup cost and complexity compared with choosing and buying individual apps.
The higher-conversion claim for Manhattan is a **vendor statement** (what the seller says). Test it on your own store.
A dropshipping-focused theme can be customized in every element. The same theme works for an elegant brand look or a playful one.
It is a free download for stores built on the **blueprint** (the course's build plan).
Pick a theme you expect to be happy with long term. Switching themes costs time that could go to revenue-generating work (work that brings in money).
Themes from established vendors that do what you need are a sound choice.

**Buy themes only** from the Shopify Theme Store or from established **theme vendors** (companies that sell themes). Unverified theme code can contain **malicious code** (harmful code) and cause problems later.
Choose a theme from the Shopify theme store or from a trusted, **certified developer** (a builder with proof of skill).
A developer who builds themes full time, with a team of about **3 to 5 people**, is a stronger choice. A person who sells a theme as a side project is a weaker choice.
Choosing a theme: criteria (continued)
Before adopting a third-party theme (one made by another company), check community discussions about the vendor's **support** quality. Poor support can leave your customizations broken.
Search the store owners' Facebook group for the theme name to see what other users report.
Shopify planned to separate theme design from store content. A theme could then be replaced without rebuilding all content. Once available, this would make theme updates faster.
It would also reduce the need for third-party **page builders** (add-on tools for building pages, such as PageFly or Shogun), which may become less useful as native (built-in) features improve.
A brand that takes branding seriously usually needs a **custom build** from a design file.
One example is a **pixel-perfect** (exact copy) conversion of a **Figma** design (a design file made in the Figma tool) into a Shopify store.
Prototyping (making a quick test version) in a page builder first, then having a developer make a polished version, is a common approach among high-revenue brands.
A **plug-and-play** store theme (one that works right after install) gets a high-converting store running fast. You do not build a website from scratch.
It reduces development time, so the focus can move to marketing and sales.
Shopify beginners do well with a theme that has many built-in features and handles most of the layout work. Its **graphics** (images) are simple to make and upload and need little design skill.
Other themes need their own graphic sizes. Confirm the chosen theme's sizes first.
For beginners without web design experience, the **Source A theme** is a strong choice. It has many features and needs little design work from the **merchant** (the store owner).
Its graphics are simple to upload because the theme handles much of the layout.
Free Shopify themes suitable for beginners include **Sense**, **Refresh** and **Dawn**. Find them under Online Store > Themes. You can use them right after sign-up.
The course material pointed to **Refresh** as a starting theme for a first build.
**Winning Hunter**'s Sales Tracker Details page (a page in a tool that tracks competitor stores) shows which Shopify theme a competitor runs. It also shows the launch date and shop URL (web address).
Note the theme when you study a competitor's build. It shows what a working store layout looks like on that platform.
Named themes
**Manhattan (Source A, version 2023)**
Status and price: Members only. The 2023 Theme Store listing note is dated 9 November 2023.
Use and notes: Built for high-ticket dropshipping. More user-friendly and somewhat faster than Charlotte. A new store should use it.

**Charlotte (Source A, meaning Source A's version)**
Status and price: Download from the members area, not from the theme store.
Use and notes: Fully capable. Loads in about 645 ms (milliseconds, a thousandth of a second). Used for the stores in the program. Switching from it is optional.

**Dawn**
Status and price: Free default.

Use and notes: Supports **Shopify 2.0** (the newer system) **drag-and-drop sections** (you move page blocks into place with the mouse).
**Debut**
Status and price: Free, older default.

Use and notes: Shows placeholder content (dummy text) and no branding. Stays listed after replacement as "Not customized yet."
**Venture**

Status and price: Free.
Use and notes: Compared against paid themes in the store listing.
**Refresh, Sense**

Status and price: Free.
Use and notes: Beginner-friendly starting themes.
**Ecomify Lite / Pro**
Status and price: Lite is free. Pro was a one-time payment of $249 when the material was made.
Use and notes: Lite lacks the **line item property** feature (extra details attached to an ordered item). That feature is part of Pro. Upgrades to the next major version were announced as about $50.

**Shrine Pro**
Status and price: Premium. One license per store.
Use and notes: Chosen because it has the most sections of the Shrine versions.
**Superstore (Pixel Union)**
Named themes (continued)
Status and price: Premium. Arrives as a zip. The version suffix (the ending that shows the version, for example superstore-v3) changes with releases.

Use and notes: Demo homepage built from editor sections.
**Avenue**
Status and price: Paid. Shown at 180 USD during a spring sale.

Use and notes: Check the current price on the store page.
**Parallax**
Status and price: Listed at $180 in the Theme Store when the material was made.
Use and notes: Demo showed full-screen video blocks (theme sections that play video), scrolling image backgrounds and large decorative images.

Paid themes are not automatically faster or more usable.
**Turbo**
Status and price: Recommended.

Use and notes: Strong support.
**Shoptimize**
Status and price: Listed in the same source.
Use and notes: Suits **direct-response** stores (stores built to make buyers act right away). It looks less premium, which can limit perceived brand quality.

**Out of the Sandbox themes**
Status and price: Roughly $300 to $500. Flex is around $500.

Use and notes: Recommended for **large-inventory stores** (stores with many products) when the budget allows. All were converted to **Online Store 2.0** (the newer Shopify store system) when recorded.

**Source A Charlotte**
Status and price: Mid-range.

Use and notes: Works as an alternative to premium Out of the Sandbox themes. It gives a professional look without the highest price.
**Shop (Pixel Union)**

Status and price: Retail around $300.
Use and notes: Budget for this cost if the theme is not included with a course or purchase.
**the Source F theme**

Status and price: Added to an existing store.
Use and notes: See the procedure below.
Shopify's Charlotte-era advice on speed said the Source A Shopify theme was faster than most free themes by default. Paid Out of the Sandbox themes were described as high-quality but expensive.
The **Online Store 2.0** theme replaces several paid apps with built-in functions. It reportedly loads in **under two seconds**. It was still in **beta** (an early test version) at the time.
Free versus paid
A **free theme** is enough for conversions unless a paid theme has built-in functions you cannot get elsewhere.
Beautiful design alone does not drive sales. Speed plus trust matter most.
Premium paid third-party themes, some costing around **500 dollars**, are not needed to start. A free theme is enough. The theme is not what makes a store profitable.
Premium themes are worth the cost because they are highly customizable, load fast and come with strong support. A store with many products benefits most from these features.
Out of the Sandbox themes are recommended for large-inventory stores when the budget allows.
Upgrading to a paid premium theme was seen as sensible once the store earns good revenue. One source bought a premium theme for about **200 USD** with a 20 USD discount.
Premium Shopify themes from paid developers can retail for around **$300**. Budget for this if the theme is not included free with a course or purchase.
Off-the-shelf (ready-made) premium themes are a far cheaper route than a fully custom theme. A custom theme can cost **thousands of dollars**.
Free **line item property code snippets** (short pieces of ready-to-paste code) exist online. You can add them to a Shopify theme by hand.

Ecomify Pro was a **one-time payment of $249** when the material was made. Lite was free. Upgrades to the next major version were announced as small fees of about **$50** instead of a new $249 payment.
Check the **current price** on the store page before buying. Sale prices can differ from standard prices.

Prices differ between sources and dates. Treat each figure as the price at the time of its source.
About **180 USD** for a Theme Store listing.

About **300 USD** for a comparable premium theme (same period).
About **200 USD** for a premium theme bought at a discount.

**300 to 500 USD** for Out of the Sandbox themes.
About **500 USD** for the high-end paid themes that a free theme replaces.
Where sources disagree
**Manhattan access:** one note dated 9 November 2023 tells you to find and download Manhattan from the Shopify Theme Store.
Other sources say Manhattan is available only to members of the program. Use the members' download link provided in the course.
**Charlotte versions:** Charlotte 1.0 was the original download from the blueprint.
Version **1.3** is the latest downloadable Charlotte version, released 21 February 2022.

Earlier Charlotte versions can be updated to it as a new theme.
**Source A version:** the newest Source A theme was last updated **12 December 2022**.
A later source named version 1.3 as current and said the course downloads carry it.
**Charlotte or Manhattan for an existing store:** a new store should use Manhattan. An existing store on Charlotte does not need to be switched.
**Speed:** older advice (2022) recommended Charlotte for speed. Later advice says Manhattan is somewhat faster than Charlotte. Use the newer comparison when choosing for a new store.
**Premium value:** for large-inventory stores, premium themes are worth the cost. For a starting store, a free theme is enough.
Use the premium argument only when the store has the volume or features to justify it.
**Publishing a new theme:** publish straight away only on a **brand-new store** with no other active theme in use.
On a store that already has visitors and sales, keep the theme **unpublished** until setup is finished.
**Password-protected stores:** a new store can be published while still **password protected** (locked behind a password page).
Visitors cannot see the live site until a **custom domain** (your own web address) is connected.
Getting the theme file
**Done For You** (a service where the provider builds the store for you): if the store was set up through a done-for-you option,
the team installs Manhattan for you. Skip the remaining build steps until you get confirmation.
The theme is already installed by the provider. The manual upload and publish steps are not needed.
Receive the theme file from the course provider before uploading. It arrives as a **zip archive** (a compressed file) by email.
Charlotte is not in the Shopify theme store. **Download it from the members area.**
The newest Source A theme version is in the members area. It was last updated **12 December 2022**.
The older Source A theme still works and does not need an upgrade. The theme is private and not in the Shopify app store. The newest version must come from the course downloads.
**Download the theme as a zip file and upload the zip directly.** Extracting the zip and uploading its folders will not work.
Shopify accepts theme files only in **.zip format**. The file has to end in.zip before you upload it. Uploading a folder or another format will not work.
The Shopify theme file must be a zip archive with a maximum size of **50 MB** (megabytes). An unzipped folder fails.
1. Click the Manhattan theme **download link** provided in the course.

2. Review the theme details on the page if you want.
3. Scroll to the **bottom** of the page.
4. Check the box to confirm your **membership status**.

5. Click **Download Manhattan** to save the ZIP file to your computer.
6. Log into your Shopify account.

7. Click **Online Store** in the main menu.
8. Click **Themes**.
9. Click **Import Theme** in the top right corner.

10. Click **Upload a zip file**.
11. Upload the Manhattan ZIP file. Click **Add File** to select it from your computer, or drag and drop the file.
12. Click **Upload File**.
13. Wait for the installation to finish. Manhattan will appear in your **Theme Library**.
14. Click the **Publish** button on the Manhattan theme. Newly uploaded themes are not published automatically.
15. Confirm that Manhattan is now your **active theme** and appears at the top of your theme list.
Theme store download procedure (dated 9 November 2023)
1. Go to the Shopify Theme Store at https://themes.shopify.com/.
2. **Find and download** the Manhattan theme (current as of November 9th, 2023).
3. Upload the theme to your Shopify store using Shopify's official documentation at https://help.shopify.com/manual/using-themes/install-themes#upload-theme.
On a Mac, downloading a.zip file can automatically unpack it into a folder.
p.h: Fixing a zip download on a Mac

p.t: The folder shows as a **blue folder icon** instead of a zip icon. Uploading that folder fails because Shopify needs the.zip file.

if macOS unzipped the theme, **re-zip the folder** (pack it into a new zip file). Other folder types fail to upload.
Fix a Mac download that was unpacked into a folder:

1. **Right-click** the blue folder.
2. Choose **Compress** (make a new zip file) with the theme file name (for example Source A Manhattan) from the menu.
3. Use the new.zip file that macOS creates for the upload.

Upload a theme to Shopify (current procedure):
1. Go to **Online Store > Themes** and open the **Theme library**.

2. Click **Add theme**.
3. Click **Upload zip file**.
4. Drag the.zip file into the upload area or select it, then click **Upload file**.
5. Wait while the message **Installing theme** appears. This takes about **30 seconds** while Shopify processes the file.
6. Check that the new theme appears in the Theme library with its name and version number, for example Manhattan version 2023.
7. Click **Publish** only if the store has no active theme in use yet. This is the case for a brand-new store.
Processing a theme file takes about **30 seconds**. The progress message **Installing theme** appears during this time.
Large theme files take a while to upload. Wait until the theme shows in the Theme library and the installation has finished. Then click **Publish**.
A theme uploaded to Shopify is **unpublished by default**. Uploading it does not change what visitors see. You can edit the new theme safely before publishing it.
Uploading a theme does **not** activate it. The previously published theme, usually the default Shopify theme, stays live until you click **Publish** on the new theme.
Theme admin upload procedure (course version)

1. Log in to your Shopify account.
2. In the left navigation, click **Online store**, then **Themes**.

3. Click **Import theme** in the top right corner.
4. Click **upload a zip file**. Then either click **add file** and select the ZIP file, or drag the ZIP file into the upload area.

5. Click **upload file** and wait for the upload to finish.
6. Find the new theme in the theme library and click **Publish** on it.
Online store > Themes > Import theme (top right) > upload a zip file > add file or drag the ZIP file in > Upload file. The uploaded theme then appears in the theme library below the active theme.
Publish the uploaded theme in the theme library to make it the live theme. Publishing **replaces** the currently active theme, such as the free default Shopify theme, with the uploaded one.
**Import theme** is the same action as Upload theme or Add theme > Upload zip file in the other sources.

1. In the Shopify admin, go to **Online Store > Themes**.
2. Click **Upload theme** under Theme library.
3. Click **Add file** and select the theme file. It must be a.zip archive. Re-zip the folder if macOS unzipped it automatically, because other folder types fail to upload.
4. Click **Upload file** and wait for the upload to finish. The theme is added **unpublished** by default. The maximum file size is 50 MB.
5. Click **Actions** on the uploaded theme. Use Customize only when editing. Do not change the code editor settings in Actions at this stage.
6. Click **Publish**, then confirm with Publish again. This replaces the current theme and makes it the active theme.
7. Preview the store using the **eyeball icon** to check the change.
Add theme procedure (2023)
Upload a new theme in the Shopify admin under Themes. Use **Add theme**, then **Upload**.

It stays unpublished and invisible to customers until you click Publish. You can customize it safely first.
Setting up a new theme without disturbing the live store:

1. In Shopify admin, open **Themes**.
2. Click **Add theme**, then **Upload theme**.
3. Customize the uploaded theme while it is unpublished.
4. Click **Publish** only when the store is ready.
Upload a new theme so it lands in the **theme library**. Make all customizations there, then click **Publish**.

The published theme replaces the live one, and the old theme moves into the library.
Check the **active theme name** in Shopify under Online Store > Themes.
1. **Buy the theme license** (the permission to use the theme) on the vendor site. Choose the number of licenses the store needs.
2. Download the theme file that the vendor emails after checkout.
3. In Shopify admin, go to **Online Store > Themes** and choose **Upload theme**. Select the zip file.
4. Uploaded themes are unpublished by default. Open the theme and choose **Edit theme** or **Publish** once it is ready.
5. Enter the **license number** from the vendor into the review app (Judge.me, an app that collects customer reviews) so reviews work.
6. Adjust the **header**, home page, collection and product page sections in the theme editor.

7. Set the logo, colors, **typography** (text styles) and button styling under **Theme settings**.
8. Check the layout in **mobile preview** before publishing.

A theme uploaded as a zip file is placed under Online Store > Themes as an **unpublished draft** (a version not yet live). It must be published before visitors see it. Use the **Edit theme** button on the draft to open the editor.
Go to **Online Store > Add Theme > Upload ZIP file**. No new Shopify account is required.
p.h: Adding the Source F theme to an existing store

p.t: Draft versus published
Install a new theme (the design template that sets how the store looks) as **unpublished**. Unpublished means hidden from customers.
Adjust it while it is unpublished. Then **publish** it when it is ready. Publish means making it the live theme, the version real customers see.

Installing a theme directly onto a live store can break the site.
When a new theme is uploaded, it goes live only as a **draft**. A draft is a hidden copy that only you can see. (2024.)

Uploading a draft does not change the current live store.
You can customize the draft. Customize means opening the editor to change colors, layout and other settings.

Then **publish** the draft when it is ready.
A new Shopify theme is installed as a draft that only you can see. Shopify is the platform the store runs on.

Design it in the draft, then **publish** it.
Installing a new theme does not carry over the design edits of the old theme.

Apps (add-on tools you install) and products do carry over.
Upload a new theme as a **draft** first, so the live store is not affected while you check it.

Uploading a theme as a draft does not change the live store.
If the new theme is published by mistake, you can **republish the old theme** to go back. Revert means undo.
Themes do not update automatically in the background once installed.
Publishing a new theme on a store that already gets traffic (visitors) and sales, before its customization is finished, can change the live site unexpectedly.
**Finish setup and customization** before publishing.
Publish a new theme **right away** only when the store is brand new and no other theme besides the default free one is in use.
If the store already has visitors and sales, keep the new theme unpublished until the remaining setup steps are complete.
Publishing a new theme **replaces the current active theme immediately**.
Until a custom domain (your own web address, such as yourbrand.com) is connected, the store can stay password protected. Password protected means visitors cannot see the live site.
The replaced theme stays listed in the Theme library. The Theme library is the list of all themes saved in your store.
It can be **published again** if the new theme needs to be reverted.
Shrine Pro setup includes **publishing the theme** while the store is still password protected.
Draft versus published (continued)

This is the step where the theme goes live behind the password.
Do not **change a working theme** just to upload products.
Uploading products is the same process for any theme, so a redesign suggested for that reason is unnecessary.
A live store with traffic does not need to switch to a newly released theme.

Upgrades only improve usability. Adopt them **when convenient**, not as an urgent change.
Switching themes is **not urgent**.
An older Source A theme (a theme from the Source A course) can keep being used until you have time to change it.
Changing to a newer theme later will not break the store if it is **not published before testing**.
Changing the theme often disrupts traffic and conversions. Conversions are visitors who buy.
So make design changes **deliberately**, mostly in a later phase of conversion rate optimization (CRO), which means improving how many visitors buy. Do not repeat them again and again.
**Avoid editing the site's code** early on. Code here means the instructions that build the site.
Custom code changes are worth it only once the business is selling and growing. The theme editor covers the launch phase. The theme editor is the visual screen for changing the look.

Test a new theme without changing the live store:
1. Go to **Online Store > Themes** in the Shopify admin, the back office where you run the store.
2. Add the theme zip to the theme library. A zip is a packed download file. The new theme appears as a draft and does not change the store.

3. Click **Customize** on the draft, then edit and preview it. Preview means checking how it looks before customers see it.
4. When it is ready, click **Publish** to make it the live theme.

Test a new theme without going live (2023):
1. **Download** the theme zip file.
2. Upload it in the Shopify admin as an unpublished theme.

3. Preview it and make changes.
4. Keep the current live theme until you decide to **publish** the new one. At that point, the current theme becomes a draft.

Publish a new theme after customizing it (2025):
1. **Upload** the new theme. It is saved as a draft.

2. Open Customize for the draft theme and change colors, the logo and other settings.
3. When satisfied, click **Publish**.
4. The new theme becomes the main theme. The old theme moves to the theme library as a draft. Menus (the navigation links), products and pages stay in place, so you do not need to recreate them.
Switching themes

Switching themes requires **redoing customizations** such as colors and homepage images.
Products do not need to be rebuilt.

Switching themes takes only a few clicks.
Custom colors and custom code do **not carry over automatically**.
The effort depends on how far the store has been changed from the default theme.
When switching themes, **products, collections, blog posts and pages are kept**. Collections are groups of products.
Logo, menus, colors, fonts, homepage images and homepage layout must be **set again**.

Switching themes changes the look, not the data. Products, pages and blogs remain.
The new theme needs only skinning (changing colors, logos and images) before publishing.

**Test the new design in draft mode** first. Draft mode means the hidden version. (2024.)
Switching themes does not change your products.

Theme customizations such as layout changes must be **applied again** in the new theme.
A theme switch to a newer Shopify theme does not require rebuilding the store.

Content pages and product pages carry over.
Colors and image placements need to be **reset** in the new theme. (2023.)

A new theme migration keeps products, pages and content.
Cosmetic items must be **reset**. These include color scheme, logo, homepage images and layout.
Switch an established store to a new theme **only if you need functions** it offers.
New stores can start on the newest version. Stores already running well can **wait** for the final release.
The Charlotte theme (an older Shopify theme) is not expected to be replaced soon.
No major update is planned in the near term. A new theme was expected around a year out, and the current one stays supported.
Changing themes, for example from Charlotte to Manhattan, has **no one-click migration**. A migration is a move of the store to a new theme.

The practical method is to keep both theme editors open side by side, on two monitors or in a split screen.
Then **move settings over manually**. (2024.)
Switching themes (continued)

Migrating to a new theme (2021):
1. **Install** the new theme as a draft so the live store is unchanged.
2. Copy over the color scheme, logo, homepage images and layout by hand. Products, pages and content carry over automatically.
3. Keep the published theme and the draft theme open side by side. Transfer things one by one.

Install a new theme (for example Manhattan) on an existing Shopify store without losing content (2024):
1. **Download** the theme first.
2. Upload it to Shopify. It is saved as a draft and does not replace the live theme.
3. In the draft, set the color scheme, logo, images, homepage and collection images, and add any custom code.
4. Products, pages and blogs carry over automatically.
5. When happy, **publish** the draft. The old theme becomes a draft and the new theme becomes active. You can toggle back at any time.

Migrating to a new theme, the checklist (2022):
1. Make changes in **draft mode**, not live.
2. Visit every page type: homepage, collections, product pages, contact, blog and checkout. Checkout is the page where customers pay.

3. Click and interact with everything.
4. Test the entire purchase process.
5. Check that all apps display correctly. For example, Klarna financing buttons. Klarna is a service that lets customers pay in installments.

6. Only **push live** after confirming everything works.
Migrating Shopify themes (2022):

1. **Create** the new theme as a draft in Shopify. This does not affect the live store.
2. Work on design changes in draft mode: colors, logo, layouts.

3. **Preview** the draft to test all pages.
4. When satisfied, **publish** the draft as the new live theme.
5. The previous theme automatically moves to draft status. You can revert to it if needed.
Switching themes (continued)
6. The product catalog, data and content remain unchanged. Only design elements are swapped.

When switching Shopify themes, **create the new theme as a draft**.
Work on design changes in the background. Then preview the draft, and **publish** it as live.
The previous theme automatically moves to draft status. You can **revert** to it at any time if needed.
Install a new Shopify theme such as Charlotte without disrupting the live store (2022):

1. **Add** the theme as a new theme in the Shopify back end, where it appears as a draft. The back end is the admin area.
2. Customize the draft for colors, logo and similar settings.

3. **Publish** it. The previous theme then becomes the draft.
Products, collections and pages transfer automatically, and **no downtime** occurs. Downtime means the store is offline.

Switching to a newer theme (2022):
1. **Upload** the new theme as a draft in Shopify.
2. Re-apply the colors, logo and custom images.
3. Products, collections and content pages carry over, so the store core does not need to be rebuilt.

Migrating a live store to a new theme without changing the live store (2024):
1. **Upload** the new theme. It is saved as a draft.

2. Customize the draft while the current theme stays live.
3. **Publish** the draft when it is ready. This makes it the live theme and turns the previous live theme into a draft.
Traffic after a theme change: the page structure and URLs (web addresses) remain identical, so traffic should not change.
If traffic drops after a theme migration, **check Google Analytics** to see where visitors came from. Google Analytics is a free tool that tracks visitors.
Check the acquisition sources. These show which source dropped: organic (free search results), paid (ads), direct (typed-in address) or referral (links from other sites).
The Charlotte theme was recommended for its **lightweight speed**. Lightweight means it loads quickly.

Charlotte loads in about **645 milliseconds**, which is already fast.
Switching to a newer theme is optional, not needed for speed alone. (2024.)
Updating a theme
A new theme version is **not an automatic update** to an existing store.

It has to be uploaded and installed like any other theme. Plan the switch and test the store before going live.
Theme updates are not applied automatically.
The developer notes what changed and how to apply it, because automatic updates could break a customized store.

Before updating a Shopify store theme, **confirm which theme version** is installed.
Ask support whether the update will keep your customizations.

Do not assume a theme update will leave custom changes intact.
Upgrading a theme without losing the live store (2020):
1. Open the Shopify admin.

2. Go to **Online Store**, then **Themes**.
3. **Upload** the newest version of the theme.

4. Adjust colors and layout in the draft. This does not change the live store.
5. Click **Publish** only when the draft is ready.

6. If needed, **republish the previous theme**.
Theme upgrades reset design choices such as colors and layout. Products and content stay.

**Plan time to restyle** after upgrading.
Use the newest version of the store theme. It should be at least as recent as the last couple of months.

Older themes can be upgraded, but the upgrade means **redoing the design**.
Update to a new theme without breaking the live store (2021):

1. **Upload** the new theme. It is saved as a draft.
2. Edit and adjust the draft until it looks right.
3. **Publish** it. The old theme remains available as an option.

If the current theme works, there is **no need to switch**.
Install the newest Source A theme version (2023):

1. Go to the members area and **download** the newest theme. It was last updated 12 December 2022.
2. In Shopify, **upload** it as a draft so customers do not see it.

3. Edit and test it in the draft.
4. When ready, **publish** the new theme and set the old one to draft.

Charlotte v1.3 is the latest downloadable version, released **21 February 2022**.
Earlier versions can be updated to it as a new theme.
Charlotte bug fixes arrive as **small code snippets**. A snippet is a short piece of code.
If a live store shows an issue, **ask support** for the code change. Do not download and rebuild the theme again.
Updating a theme (continued)

The 1.2 to 1.3 Charlotte update consisted of **small bug fixes**, not new features.
No detailed change log (a written list of changes) was available at that time.
Shopify 2.0 is the newer theme system. It redesigned the theme customizer, so the editor looks different from earlier versions.
**Drag-and-drop sections** across the whole page work only on themes whose developers have updated them to support it. At launch, very few themes did.

Dawn (a free Shopify theme) supports the Shopify 2.0 drag-and-drop sections feature.
At launch, Dawn was one of **very few themes** to do so.
**Check which themes support the feature** before planning a redesign around it.
Before switching to a Shopify 2.0 theme, **ask your theme developer** for their timeline for supporting the update.
Themes from developers who rarely update may never gain the new features.
Updating a theme usually **wipes customizations**. This includes custom code for SEO (search engine ranking) and custom front-end elements that customers see. Front-end means the part visitors see.

**Before updating, record** where each piece of code was inserted and how, so you can restore it.
A lightly customized store can switch to a new theme with little work.
A store with years of layered changes needs a developer or a careful audit. An audit is a full check.
A theme update can also be a good chance to **rebuild the store from a clean slate**.
Hard-coded edits (changes written directly into the theme code) are **not carried over** when a new theme version is migrated.
**Plan to reapply** custom code changes after a theme upgrade, and keep a record of them.
A Chrome extension (a small add-on for the Chrome browser) migrates a store's theme changes into a new theme version.

It does not move hard-coded edits.
It is a helpful tool when a theme update is released.

Theme licensing emails that claim a problem are often **phishing**. Phishing is a fake email that steals logins. (2025.)
Check that the sender ends in **@shopify.com**.
Emails can be spoofed, meaning the sender name can be faked. So **verify through the Shopify support page**, not by replying to the email.
Backups and exporting
Create a **backup** before editing the store code. A deleted product page can disrupt daily sales.
Ask for help with code changes rather than experimenting on the live store.
Editing theme code without a full backup can break a live product page with **no easy way back**.
Copy the **complete original file** into a document before changing anything.
Rewind Backups is a Shopify backup app. It stores copies of store data such as products, themes and orders. (2024.)

Use it to **restore the store** after accidental changes or deletions.
Before switching the theme:
1. **Back up the store** before switching the theme.
2. Change the theme in Shopify. Products do not need to be uploaded again.
3. **Redo all custom code and customizations** from the old theme, because they are removed with it.

Shopify theme code can be exported from one store and imported into another to keep the same design.
Look up **Shopify theme export** for the steps.

To go back, **republish the previous theme** in the Theme library.
The previous theme remains available as a draft or in the library after a switch.
Theme support and safety
A discount code that cannot be removed should be handled by the theme's support team if the theme is their own.

For other Shopify themes, **Shopify support** can access and change the store directly.
A store built on a Shopify theme such as Dawn can look different on Windows and Mac.

Custom code changes can break the store.
A problem with a store connection can take a long time to diagnose.

The Shopify support team can send a **fix video**.
Shopify support can help with store problems by sending a video that shows how to fix the issue.
This option can **save hours** compared with troubleshooting alone.
If a styling option such as a tab border color cannot be found in the Shopify theme settings, **do not guess** at code changes.
Ask the theme provider's support instead. The change may need the designer.
Theme code is edited in the **edit.html and edit.css** files in the Shopify theme editor. HTML is the page layout code. CSS is the styling code.
This is the route for HTML and CSS changes that fall outside the Customizer's built-in options. The Customizer is the theme editor.

The Source A Manhattan theme is the Shopify theme used in this store build.
Its Customizer offers **built-in settings** for font, colors, layout and content.
**Edit theme code only after testing on a duplicate theme**. A duplicate is a copy used for testing.
The storefront theme in the demo was the live theme. A broken Liquid edit on the live theme affects real customers immediately. Liquid is Shopify's code language.
Before adopting a third-party theme, **check community discussions** about the vendor's support quality. A vendor is the company that sells the theme.
Shopify's approach to theme safety is to **buy only from the Shopify Theme Store** or established vendors. The Theme Store is Shopify's official theme shop.

Check each theme's developer and update history before choosing it.
Editing theme code, the safety checklist:

**Back up the complete original file** first.
**Create a backup** before editing the store code.
**Test on a duplicate theme** before editing the live one.

**Ask for help** with code changes rather than experimenting on the live store.
**Avoid editing the site's code** early on.
Shrine Pro setup
Premium themes (paid themes) are worth choosing when they include conversion elements. Then the store needs fewer paid apps.

Shrine Pro was chosen because it has the most sections of the Shrine theme versions.
**One license is enough** for one store. A license is permission to use a paid theme.
The email address entered at checkout for a Shrine license must be **correct**.
The license keys (codes that unlock the theme) are delivered to that address. A wrong address can prevent access to the keys.

Set up a premium Shrine Pro theme in Shopify, in this order:
1. Open the Shrine Pro page and click **Get started**.

2. Select **one license**, because only one store is being built, and click **Add to cart**.
3. Click **Checkout**.
4. Check that the email address entered at checkout is **correct**.
5. Accept the terms and conditions, click **Complete purchase**, and then click **Continue**.
6. Open the email from Shrine that contains the license keys, and click **Open Shrine Dashboard**. The dashboard is your Shrine account page.

7. If there is no Shrine account yet, click **register** and create an account, then log in.
8. Click **Next step**, then click **Add key**, and enter the license key to activate it.
9. In Shopify, go to **Settings > Domains** and copy the myshopify.com URL. This is the free web address Shopify gives your store.

10. In Shrine, go to **Settings > Accounts > Whitelist your URLs**. Whitelist means adding addresses to an allowed list. Paste the myshopify.com URL into the Shopify URL field, with https:// in front.

11. Copy the custom domain of the store from Shopify **Settings > Domains**. Paste it into the Main URL field, with https:// in front. If a second website URL exists, add it in the Secondary URL field the same way.
12. Click **Save and generate token**, then copy the authentication token and store it safely. A token is a secret code that links the theme to your store.
13. **Download** the theme zip file from Shrine.
14. In Shopify, go to **Online Store > Themes**, click **Import theme**, upload the zip file, and select the Shrine Pro theme file. Wait until the upload has finished.

15. Click **Publish** to make the theme live, even though the store is still password protected.
16. Click **Customize** to open the theme editor and add sections.
Choosing a theme

**Start with a free Shopify theme** and keep the store simple.
Keep a clear product page, a short homepage, and clean images.
A beginner should start with a simple, quickly built store theme, such as a basic version of Shrine, rather than spending time on advanced themes.

Elixir suits operators who already know how to **build a proper website**.
Beautify is a popular **paid** theme.

Its look is common among dropshipping stores, so it is **not required**. Dropshipping means selling products you do not stock yourself.

The choice of theme matters **much less than launching fast**.
Small custom code changes on a simple theme are enough to make a store look distinct from the average store.
Cracked or pirated themes (illegally copied versions) can hide bugs or malicious code (harmful software hidden in the file) that can break the store.
**Buy** themes from the official source or a verified reseller (a seller that has been checked as trustworthy).
Uploading a theme zip file
After a Shrine Pro zip file (a compressed theme package) is uploaded to Shopify (the online store platform),
it appears in the theme library (your list of themes) as **shrine-theme-pro**, version 1.5.4, labeled Just added.
Shopify states that uploaded themes are visible only to the **store team** (the people who run the store) until one of them is published (made live for shoppers).
A theme can be **published** (made live) while the store is still password protected (locked behind a password for visitors).
p.h: Draft and published themes and password protection

p.t:
This lets you prepare the theme before the store opens to visitors.
The password protection stays active until it is removed.
In Shopify, the password protection of a store is managed on the theme card (the box that shows one theme) under **Online Store > Themes**.
The theme card shows the buttons Edit password and **Remove password**, and displays Password protected while the protection is active.
Moving to a new Shopify store while reusing content (using again what you already built):
p.h: Moving to a new Shopify store while reusing content

p.t: 1. **Create** the new store with another email (a different email address).
2. Export (save a copy of) the theme from the online store section and import (load) it into the new store.
3. Export and import the customer and SMS lists (lists of customer contacts for text messages), and set up the email settings and apps (add-on tools) **again**.

Shopify's export and import buttons handle the data.
4. **Rebuild** any settings that do not transfer, such as logos and notification email settings.
